prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of flat electronic bands in bilayer graphene at a magic twist angle and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep the single-part magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene configuration with MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Bistritzer, and my preference is firmer than in round 1 because the chair's summary shows that no one disputes the core observation or its reproduction by independent groups. The scientific structure is what matters to me. A continuum band-structure calculation gave a quantitative flat-band condition at a specific twist angle, and seven years later experiment found correlated insulators and superconductivity in exactly that regime, with one tunable parameter controlling bandwidth against interaction. As an electronic-structure theorist I regard this as the rare case in which a model Hamiltonian derived from the lattice, not fitted afterwards, set the experimental agenda. The result has carried to other moire platforms and to fractional Chern states, which indicates a robust discovery and not a sample-specific curiosity. On the chair's question about the pairing mechanism, I would support the same configuration if the superconductivity turned out to be conventional: the discovery is that flat-band physics is realised and controllable in a bilayer, and a mundane pairing mechanism would not undo that. The citation should therefore claim only the prediction and the observed states, and say nothing about mechanism.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection, which I take seriously, is timing together with credit. The field is about eight years old, the phase diagram is still being rewritten, and device-to-device variation from twist-angle disorder means some published claims are sample-specific. A three-name set leaves out Yuan Cao as first author of the 2018 papers, Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto for earlier twisted-bilayer band-flattening theory, and other moire experimental groups. I have not verified the priority history from a source and am relying on recollection. If the committee judges that the robust core and the sample-dependent behaviour are not yet separable, waiting a few years is a defensible position, and B045 is then the mature fallback. I do not think the evidence supports that this year, but I record the reasoning.

responses.point: Kroll argues that lattice clocks are a measurement result, not only engineering, that the Katori and Ye credit is the cleanest on the shortlist, and that a citation should say what is specific to lattices as against ion clocks.
responses.response: I accept all three points and they keep B045 as my first alternative. I do not read the clocks as inferior science: sub-1e-18 agreement between independent institutes is a hard, verified result, and the many-atom regime is a genuine distinction from ion clocks. Where we differ is the criterion. The chair asked what new physics, as opposed to new accuracy, the clocks have revealed, and the answer so far, tests of relativity and constants at tighter bounds and many-body clock shifts, is a refinement of known physics in an established area, whereas B038 opened a new class of correlated states with a controllable knob. I weigh that breadth difference, with the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes as a mild further factor, but I treat it as judgement and not a decisive scientific argument. I also note that the redefinition of the second has not occurred and I give it no weight.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the clock's maturity and unchanged interpretation over two decades contrast with a field whose interpretation is still moving, and that twist-angle disorder makes quantitative cross-laboratory comparison weaker than for clocks.
responses.response: The point on maturity is correct and is the best case against my position. Where I disagree is on what needs to be stable. The claim a citation would carry is the existence of flat-band correlated insulating and superconducting states at the predicted angle, and that has been reproduced by many groups, even though phase-boundary details vary between devices. Quantitative agreement at the 1e-18 level is the right standard for a clock but not the right standard for a phase of matter, where qualitative reproducibility of the phase diagram and its dependence on the twist angle is what counts. I accept that the interpretation of the superconducting state may still move, and for that reason I want the citation to avoid mechanism entirely. That is a wording safeguard, and it answers more of the maturity worry than it concedes.

responses.point: Olsson names as her most serious concern that B038 could be slightly early because sample and twist-angle disorder questions have not fully separated robust physics from sample-dependent behaviour, while also arguing that independent reproducibility already makes the discovery secure.
responses.response: I share both halves of her position and I resolve them the same way: the robust core is established, the periphery is not, and the citation should be limited to the core. Her materials point is useful to me as a theorist, because the flat-band condition itself is a lattice property that does not depend on the details of any one sample, and that is why the prediction holds up while individual device claims vary. I would add one caution to her argument, which is that reproducibility in different laboratories is evidence for the correlated states, not for any particular reading of them. So I back the observation-based wording, and if the committee wants more time on the sample-dependence question I see it as a real argument for B045 this year and not a trivial one.

responses.point: Mehlig says the discovery is firm even though the pairing mechanism is not, and that the Bistritzer-MacDonald paper is the decisive prediction, with Cao's role acknowledged through the experimental discovery wording.
responses.response: I agree that the Bistritzer-MacDonald paper is the decisive prediction, because it gave the quantitative magic-angle condition and not only a trend toward band narrowing. I do not fully agree that the wording can absorb Cao's role: the citation can say the experimental discovery and still leave a first author unnamed, and that is a real cost of the three-name limit that we should state plainly in the final record, not describe as settled. I would also not lean on the earlier statements that the credit is clean. The earlier twisted-graphene band theory is outside the set, and I rely on recollection for that history. My position is that the allocation is defensible and contested, and that this is acceptable for a discovery of this size, but it is not unproblematic.

uncertainties: Whether the committee should treat an eight-year-old field with an open superconducting mechanism as ready, and whether the sample-dependence of some claims is large enough to justify waiting.

Whether the three-name set is acceptable given that Yuan Cao, Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto and other moire groups are outside it; my account of the priority history is from recollection and unverified.
How much weight to give breadth of a new field over the cleanliness and maturity of B045, which I regard as a judgement and not a scientific fact.
My view of B037 (DMFT) as a method with the Metzner credit problem rests on recalled attribution history that I have not checked.
statement.conflict_note: My profile records no connection to MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero or Bistritzer, and no conflict is apparent for B038 or B045. B037 (DMFT) is close to my own work on DFT and correlated-electron methods, so I would flag methodological proximity and could defer if the committee takes it up; it is now only an alternative. I have no documented personal tie to any credited person.
